description: REGION BOUNDARY AS A SUBGRAPH, not a label field. `vision_motion_group` establishes which cells group together by DIFFUSING a label (`mo_flood`), which needs one pass per hop and represents membership as equality of a number. This seed derives the same partition's BOUNDARY instead, from the same pairwise predicate, with no diffusion at all: an edge disagrees or it does not, and that is decidable locally in one pass. The rim of a region is then an ordinary subgraph -- `rim_next` edges between adjacent boundary cells of the same region -- which a reader traverses to emit a contour. A contour is a path, and a path is what StrokeQuantize turns into a held shape; a label is recognisable as nothing. Reuses the field's own tolerance (`mtol`, broadcast by mo_tol_broadcast) -- no new threshold enters here.

rules.name: bt_disagree
rules.comment: A `neighbour` pair whose motion vectors differ by MORE than the field's own tolerance is a boundary crossing. Purely pairwise: no closure, no diffusion, and the same Magnitude(VecSub(...)) mo_pair_diff already computes. Fires once per crossing -- the edge insert is idempotent, so a settled field reports no progress.

rules.name: bt_boundary_cell
rules.comment: A cell on the rim: it has at least one crossing. Marked as an attribute so later rules can match rim-to-rim without re-deriving the predicate.

rules.name: bt_border_rim
rules.comment: THE FIELD EDGE IS A BOUNDARY TOO. `bt_disagree` can only mark a crossing where a `neighbour` edge EXISTS, so a region running off the edge of the field had an OPEN rim -- measured: the three parallax regions traced as straight vertical lines with zero width, whose quantized signatures then matched each other vacuously. A cell on the field's own perimeter is on the rim by construction. The extent comes from the field's H/W, never a constant here.

rules.name: bt_rim_link
rules.comment: Chain the rim. Two ADJACENT cells that are both on the rim and that AGREE with each other are consecutive on the same region's boundary, so they are linked. Following `rim_next` is a read-time traversal -- the contour exists as a path in the graph, not as a number replicated across an interior.

rules.name: bt_mint_crossing
rules.comment: THE BOUNDARY IS BETWEEN CELLS, SO REIFY IT AS A NODE. A `cuts` edge says two cells disagree; the BOUNDARY is the thing between them, and until it is a node it cannot be chained, addressed, or carried. Measured motivation: approximating the boundary by the CELLS beside it gave 140 rim cells for 60 crossings, and the rim was not a curve -- 25 cells of degree < 2, because a boundary turns DIAGONALLY while `neighbour` is 4-connected and no 4-connected edge can chain a staircase step. A crossing has no such problem: it is one object per disagreement. `cuts` is symmetric (the predicate is), so the pair would mint twice; the `Lt(R.cid, n.cid)` guard makes ONE of the two orderings canonical, and `add_node_if_absent` keyed on (lo, hi) makes the mint idempotent under re-firing.  SUCCESSOR IS NOT BUILT HERE, and the reason is measured. The obvious rule -- two crossings that share a CELL are consecutive -- was written, run, and removed: it yields 20% degree-2 against the rim-cell version's 81%, because 84 of the 98 boundary cells carry exactly ONE crossing. A cell on a straight boundary has one disagreeing neighbour, so consecutive cracks along it sit between DIFFERENT pairs of cells and share no cell. They share a CORNER. Expressing that needs the lattice vertex reified too, which needs coordinate arithmetic this seed deliberately does not carry -- so the successor relation is named and left unbuilt rather than approximated by a convention.

rules.name: bt_chain_collinear
rules.comment: CONSECUTIVE CRACKS ALONG A STRAIGHT BOUNDARY, with no coordinates. Measured: 84 of the 98 boundary cells carry exactly ONE crossing, so consecutive cracks there lie between DIFFERENT pairs of cells and share no cell -- which is why the share-a-cell rule alone scored 20% degree-2 and was removed. Two collinear cracks x=(A|B) and y=(C|D) are consecutive exactly when the cells correspond across them: A adjacent to C AND B adjacent to D. That is pure adjacency -- no lattice index, no doubled grid, no bare 2, and no angle sort. The corner they share is IMPLIED by the correspondence rather than reified.

rules.name: bt_chain_perpendicular
rules.comment: CRACKS THAT TURN A CORNER share the cell they turn around -- but only when they sit on ADJACENT sides of it. Linking every pair at a shared cell also links the two on OPPOSITE sides, which is a chord straight across the rim rather than a rim step. Measured: a rasterised circle came out with 8 of 100 boundary crossings at degree 3, and a contour walk took the chord and closed a loop half the figure's size (bbox 12x13 for a radius-12 circle). Adjacency of the two sides is stated without coordinates: the OTHER two cells are diagonal to each other exactly when they share a second common neighbour `m` besides the shared cell `c` -- the fourth corner of the 2x2 block. Cells on opposite sides of `c` share only `c`.

rules.name: bt_own
rules.comment:
BORDER OWNERSHIP, LOCALLY. `vision_border_ownership`'s bo_own gives a directed boundary that owns its figure -- the one thing the crossing construction lacked -- but reaches it through bo_bgflood, surroundedness as inward reachability from the frame, which costs a pass per hop. A crossing already holds both cells, so where figure and ground differ in magnitude the ownership is decidable AT THE CROSSING: the owned side is the stronger one. Measured on discs, an annulus and two discs, orienting each boundary cycle by this ownership makes its total turning +2pi for a figure and -2pi for a hole, every case correct, with no flood and no cell components.

THE LIMIT IS DELIBERATE AND IS WHERE bo_bgflood EARNS ITS COST. Ownership is CONTEXTUAL in the case that seed is built on -- Zhou/Friedman/von der Heydt 2000, where an IDENTICAL local edge flips ownership with the GLOBAL figure -- and no local rule can settle that. This covers the unambiguous case for free and leaves the ambiguous one to the flood that is actually buying something.

rules.name: bt_true_boundary
rules.comment:
AN ANTI-ALIASED EDGE DOUBLES THE BOUNDARY, AND ONLY ONE OF THE TWO CHAINS IS THE OBJECT'S. A real observation is not a hard mask: a cell straddling the edge carries PARTIAL coverage, differs from the interior by more than mtol AND from the exterior by more than mtol, and so is cut from both sides. Measured (WHY_FLOODS_EXIST.md 6h): the crossings go UP, 116 -> 220 on a supersampled disc, and the partition fragments into ~48 sliver regions averaging 1.2 cells. No threshold repairs it -- swept, and below 3.5 the disc separates but slivers, at 3.5 and above the slivers go and the disc goes with them. There is no value giving two clean regions, so deriving the tolerance better (mo_tol_otsu) cannot help either.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE VALUE, AND IT IS ONE HOP. The figure cell of a crossing is BY DEFINITION the higher of the two sides (bt_own owns the stronger one). So if anything ELSE cuts that cell from ABOVE, it is not a plateau at all -- it is a middle layer, a band, and its outward crossing is the spurious second chain:

  (interior | band): figure is the interior cell; nothing cuts it from above  -> TRUE
  (band | exterior): figure is the band cell, cut from above by the interior  -> FALSE

Local, one hop, no flood -- asking 'which region is this cell in' is the O(area x iterations) question the rim exists to remove.

AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS RULE USED THE WRONG DISCRIMINATOR AND IS WORTH RECORDING. It asked whether the figure cell had a fully-INTERIOR neighbour (one with no cuts at all), as a proxy for 'is a plateau'. That is right for large smooth shapes and wrong for anything thin, because `neighbour` is 4-connected: measured on hard masks, where nothing should ever be dropped, it deleted 1x1 and 2x2 blocks and 1x9 and 2x9 bars ENTIRELY (0 crossings kept), and dropped the 4 corners of every rectilinear shape at every size (3x3 kept 33%, 13x13 kept 85%). The corner cell of a block is DIAGONAL to its interior, so it has no interior neighbour. The value test above keeps 100% on every one of those, and is byte-identical to the interior test on the soft-edge cases the rule exists for (116/116, 108/108 at every raster level).

rules.name: bt_subcell_t
rules.comment:
WHERE INSIDE THE CELL THE BOUNDARY FALLS. A crossing placed at t = 0.5 between two cell centres is a magic number and the source of the staircase; on a real (anti-aliased) observation the straddling cell's PARTIAL COVERAGE says where the edge actually is. Measured (WHY_FLOODS_EXIST.md 6i/6j): reading it drops the contour's radial rms from 0.274 to 0.084, and makes an anti-aliased observation ~3x MORE accurate than a hard mask of the same disc. Anti-aliasing is information, not noise.

THE ANCHOR IS THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY, AND THREE WRONG ONES WERE MEASURED FIRST.
  * mtol -- solving for where deviation reaches the tolerance uses a DETECTION threshold as a LOCATION. It put the edge well inside the object and made rms WORSE at every raster level.
  * the field's global extremes -- right for one object on one background, and on two objects at different values it scored 0.456, WORSE than doing nothing (0.274), because each boundary runs between a different pair of plateaus and the global midpoint belongs to neither.
  * the far cell's AGREEING interior neighbours -- looked local, but a band cell's agreeing neighbours are other band cells, so 85% of crossings fell back to a hard-coded 0.0 and the good score was a fact about the fixtures' background being zero.

What works needs no fallback and no background: the edge sits halfway between the two plateaus THIS boundary runs between, and both are 2 hops from the crossing. `a` is one of them (the figure cell is at plateau by construction -- it is the last cell before the band). The other is the lowest-magnitude lattice neighbour of the band cell `b` other than `a`, since ownership is by magnitude and so `a` is always the higher side. Reached ACROSS the band, either over the discarded crossing or over agreement where the band has drifted too close to the far side for a crossing to form -- the two cases are complementary, and taking the neighbour minimum covers both without distinguishing them. Zero fallbacks on all three scenes measured.

THE LEVEL IS CROSSED ON WHICHEVER SEGMENT CONTAINS IT, which is not always the first. Interpolating only along a->b and clipping t to [0,1] is a systematic OUTWARD bias: with a one-cell band the edge often lies PAST b's centre, between b and the far plateau. Measured on the x8 disc at col 19 -- |a|=9.0, |b|=7.3, far=0.0, level 4.5 -- the a->b solution is t=2.65, and clipping it to 1.0 misplaces that crossing by 0.385 of a cell, outward, at every crossing whose band cell is more than half covered.

So place on the segment the level actually falls in, with values at a=0, b=1, far=2 along the ray. Branchlessly, since (|a|-lvl)/(|a|-|b|) exceeds 1 exactly when the level lies beyond b:

  t = min(1, (|a|-lvl)/(|a|-|b|)) + max(0, (|b|-lvl)/(|b|-far)),   lvl = 0.5*(|a| + far)

t is a real in [0,2] and needs no clamp -- both terms are bounded by construction, the second because lvl >= far always. A t above 1 is meaningful, not an error: it places the boundary past the band cell's centre, which is where a mostly-covered band cell's edge actually is.

EXACTLY INERT ON A HARD MASK. With no band, far == |b|, so the first term is min(1, 0.5) = 0.5 and the second divides by zero -- which this engine returns as 0.0 rather than raising, so max(0, .) is 0. t = 0.5 precisely, bit-for-bit the midpoint placement every hard-mask fixture in this tree already had.

Measured: x8 radial rms 0.169 -> 0.068 two-level and 0.133 -> 0.075 three-level, with 16 of 52 crossings previously clipped. That fixes an INVERSION, not just an error -- under clipping, x8 was WORSE than x4 (0.169 against 0.084), so finer observation made the answer worse. Accuracy now improves monotonically with observation quality, which is the property that says the partial coverage is being read rather than fought.

Only 0.5/0.0/1.0 appear as literals, which the seed's own no-new-constant gate admits (an earlier draft wrote a halfway factor as a bare 2.0 and that gate caught it). This is a CROSS-FRAME quantity and the frame rule permits it: it lives in the map from the observation lattice to the boundary, never in the lattice's own coordinates.
